232.title: Pirkei Avot
232.hook: a short tractate of sayings, read on summer Shabbat afternoons for centuries
232.howItsDone: A chapter of Pirkei Avot is customarily studied each Shabbat afternoon from Passover, in some communities through the summer; each chapter is traditionally introduced with the line that all Israel has a share in the world to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we closed camp four: fourteen Torah portions, read one at a time, and a line to take with you, the cycle keeps turning. Today, camp five begins. The depths: the wisdom underneath. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Something a grandmother said at a kitchen table. A line from a coach. A sticky note on the fridge that's been there so long it's gone yellow. A few sentences like that can carry a person a long way. They're short, they're portable, and they show up when they're needed. Jewish tradition has a whole little book of those sentences. It's not long. You could read it in an afternoon. And an afternoon is when it's customarily read: on Saturday afternoons, in the long, slow light of summer. Today: the book of sayings.
screen: `A SENTENCE YOU LIVE BY.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF THEM.` → `SUMMER SATURDAY AFTERNOONS.`

segments.voice: It's called Pirkei Avot. Chapters of the fathers, or, as it's often called in English, the Ethics of the Fathers. Avot, fathers, means the founding teachers, the sages who shaped Jewish life. It's part of the Mishnah, the great collection of Jewish oral law, gathered, tradition says, by Rabbi Judah the Prince. The Mishnah is mostly law: how to keep the Sabbath, how to settle a lawsuit, how to plant a field. Avot is the strange one. Almost no law at all. Just sayings, passed from teacher to student, each with the teacher's name attached. And here's a curious detail. The rabbis didn't place it in the section about prayer or holidays. They put it in the section on damages and courts. One explanation: the people who judge others most need to hear it. A custom grew of reading one chapter each Shabbat afternoon between Passover and Shavuot, six chapters, one Sabbath at a time. Some communities keep going all summer, around and around, until the fall holidays. It's printed in traditional prayer books. You may already know a line from it without knowing where it came from. Hillel's three questions, for example: if I'm not for myself, who will be? If I'm only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? That's Avot. Over the next weeks, we'll read it the way it's meant to be read. One saying at a time. Slowly.
screen: `CHAPTERS OF THE FATHERS.` · `A MISHNAH WITH ALMOST NO LAW.` · `PLACED AMONG THE COURTS.` · `ONE CHAPTER, ONE SHABBAT.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN SMALL SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one saying slowly. Take Hillel's three questions. Settle, and breathe. First: if I'm not for myself, who will be? Let it sit. Then: if I'm only for myself, what am I? Let that one sit too. Then: if not now, when? Don't answer them. Just turn them over, one at a time, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Pirkei Avot. Chapters of the fathers: the Mishnah's small book of sayings, read on summer Sabbath afternoons.
Your line: wisdom in small sayings. Today, pick one short sentence, Hillel's or your grandmother's, and carry it with you until tonight. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: The chain (Avot 1:1)
233.hook: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on: Joshua, elders, prophets, the Great Assembly
233.howItsDone: Jewish learning is traditionally passed from teacher to student, and quoting a teaching in the name of the one who said it is a valued practice, which Avot itself praises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pirkei Avot: the Mishnah's little book of sayings, read on summer afternoons. Your line was wisdom in small sayings. Did you carry one sentence all day? Today, we open it to the very first line. Day two hundred thirty-three.

In a relay race, nobody runs the whole distance. Each runner carries the baton for one stretch, then reaches out and hands it on. Drop it at the handoff, and the race is over. The runners don't own the baton. They keep it moving. A book of wisdom could open with its best advice. This one doesn't. Before a single piece of advice, Pirkei Avot stops to answer a question: where did this come from? Who handed it to whom? Today: the chain.
screen: `A RELAY RACE.` → `THE HANDOFF.` → `WHERE DID THIS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Avot, in paraphrase. Moses received Torah from Sinai, and handed it to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders. The elders to the prophets. And the prophets handed it to the men of the Great Assembly. That's it. A list of hands. Two Hebrew verbs carry the whole thing. Kibbel: he received. And masar: he handed over. Kibbel shares its root with the word kabbalah, which at first simply meant tradition: what's been received. And masorah, the word for tradition handed down, is usually traced to masar. Notice a few things the rabbis noticed. It says Moses received Torah, without the word the. Some commentators read that as deliberate: not just the written scroll, but the teaching, the explanations, the way to live it. The oral part, which you can only get from a person. And every link is a person. Joshua, Moses's student. The elders who led after him. The prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest. And the Great Assembly, which tradition says gathered in Ezra's time, after the exile in Babylon. By the end of this chapter, the chain will run all the way down to named rabbis, teacher after teacher. And there's a reason Avot begins here. Everything that follows, be patient, be kind, find a teacher, isn't one clever person's opinion. It arrived through hands. Which means that the day you teach anyone anything, you're a link too.
screen: `MOSES RECEIVED TORAH FROM SINAI.` · `KIBBEL AND MASAR.` · `JOSHUA, ELDERS, PROPHETS, ASSEMBLY.` · `EVERY LINK IS A PERSON.` · then, large: `HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank one of your teachers. Settle, and breathe. Think back to someone who handed you something that stuck. Not always a classroom teacher. A boss, an aunt, an older kid on the bus, a coach who told you the truth. Picture them. What did they hand you? Now trace it one link back: who do you think handed it to them? Hold both of them for a moment, gratefully. The bell holds the time.
The chain. Avot's first line: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, hand to hand, to Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Great Assembly.
Your line: handed down. Today, send a short thank-you to one person who taught you something, and tell them what it was. Day two hundred thirty-three.

234.title: Be slow to judge (Avot 1:1)
234.hook: the Great Assembly: be deliberate in judgment, raise many students, build a fence round the Torah
234.howItsDone: Jewish law sets out careful procedures for courts, including questioning witnesses closely and, in capital cases, delaying any guilty verdict until the next day, and Avot's call to judge deliberately is often applied to everyday life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and it was handed down, all the way to the Great Assembly. Did you thank a teacher? Today, that last link finally speaks. Day two hundred thirty-four.

It takes about a second. You see a screenshot, a headline, a neighbor's car parked badly, a coworker's short email. And the verdict is in. Guilty. Rude. Lazy. Clueless. We judge faster than we breathe, and the internet has made it a sport. Now picture a council of sages, the Great Assembly, at the end of that long chain from Sinai. They've been handed everything. And when Avot finally gives them a voice, the very first word of advice they pass on is about speed.
screen: `THE ONE-SECOND VERDICT.` → `GUILTY, RUDE, LAZY.` → `THE FIRST ADVICE IN AVOT.`

segments.voice: The men of the Great Assembly, Avot says, said three things. Be deliberate in judgment. Raise up many students. And make a fence around the Torah. Three short lines, and the first one is our word today. In Hebrew, hevu metunim ba-din. Metunim means slow, measured, patient. It's the kind of slowness of someone who takes a second look. They were speaking first to judges, the people who decide real cases. And Jewish law built that slowness into its courts. The Mishnah says that in a capital case, the old high court could acquit a person on the same day, but it could not convict on the same day. A guilty verdict had to wait until tomorrow, so the judges would sleep on it and look for any merit they'd missed. Mercy could be quick. Condemnation had to be slow. The other two sayings fit around this one. Raise up many students: don't hoard what you know. One old story says the school of Shammai wanted to teach only the worthy, and the school of Hillel said teach everyone. And make a fence around the Torah: add a little margin of care, so you don't stumble over the line itself. But the order matters. Before students, before fences: slow down. Most of us aren't judges in a court. But we judge all day long. Our kids, our partners, strangers on a train. The first advice of the sages is simply this: whatever verdict you're about to reach, let it wait a moment longer.
screen: `THREE THINGS FROM THE ASSEMBLY.` · `METUNIM — SLOW AND MEASURED.` · `ACQUIT TODAY, CONVICT TOMORROW.` · `STUDENTS AND A FENCE.` · then, large: `JUDGE SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: slow down one judgment. Settle, and breathe. Think of a verdict you reached recently, fast. About a coworker, a relative, a stranger, someone online. Put it on hold, like the old court. Ask: what might I not know? What would a good lawyer for this person say? You don't have to change your mind. Just let the verdict wait until tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Metunim. Measured, patient, slow to decide: the word behind the Great Assembly's first saying in Avot, be deliberate in judgment.
Your line: judge slowly. Today, the next time you feel a verdict forming about someone, count to ten, and look for one thing in their favor. Day two hundred thirty-four.

235.title: Three pillars (Avot 1:2)
235.hook: Simon the Just: the world stands on Torah, worship and deeds of kindness
235.howItsDone: Torah study, daily prayer and gemilut chasadim structure much of traditional Jewish life, and Simon the Just's saying is also sung, in Hebrew, as a song: al shloshah devarim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Assembly's first advice: metunim, be deliberate in judgment. Your line was judge slowly. Did you let one verdict wait? Today, one of the last members of that Assembly gets his own saying. Day two hundred thirty-five.

Try sitting on a two-legged stool. You can do it, for a while, if you concentrate, with your feet planted. But the minute you relax, you tip. Add a third leg and suddenly you can sit there all afternoon without thinking about it. Three is the smallest number that stands on its own. A lot of lives are two-legged stools. All work and worship, no kindness. All kindness, no learning. Leaning hard, one bad day from tipping over. An old sage named Simon had a saying about what the whole world rests on. Today: the three legs.
screen: `A TWO-LEGGED STOOL.` → `THREE STANDS ON ITS OWN.` → `WHAT THE WORLD RESTS ON.`

segments.voice: Simon the Just, Shimon HaTzaddik, was, tradition says, a high priest, and Avot says he was one of the last of the Great Assembly. His saying: on three things the world stands. On Torah. On avodah, worship. And on gemilut chasadim, deeds of loving-kindness. Torah is learning: studying, asking, understanding. Avodah, in Simon's day, meant the service in the Temple in Jerusalem, the offerings the priests brought there. Gemilut chasadim is kindness you do with your hands and time: visiting the sick, comforting mourners, lending without interest, helping a bride, burying the dead. Then something unthinkable happened. Rome destroyed the Temple. One of the three pillars fell. How does the world stand now? The rabbis gave two answers. First, avodah became prayer. The Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart. Second, an old story tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai walking past the ruins with his student, who cried: the place where our sins were atoned is destroyed. And the teacher said, don't grieve, we have another way, just as good: deeds of loving-kindness. And he quoted the prophet Hosea, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." So the three legs are still there. Learning, prayer, kindness. And the stool only stands when all three touch the ground.
screen: `SIMON THE JUST, HIGH PRIEST.` · `TORAH, AVODAH, KINDNESS.` · `ROME DESTROYS THE TEMPLE.` · `I DESIRE MERCY, NOT SACRIFICE.` · then, large: `THREE LEGS TO STAND ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one of each today. Settle, and breathe. First leg, learning: what's one thing you'll read or ask about today? Second leg, worship or attention: when will you pause, for a prayer if you pray, or a quiet minute if you don't? Third leg, kindness: whose day can you make lighter with your hands or your time? Picture all three. The bell holds the time.
Three pillars. Simon the Just's saying in Avot: the world stands on Torah, on worship, and on deeds of loving-kindness.
Your line: three legs to stand on. Before bed tonight, check: did I learn something, pause for something, and do something kind? Day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Not for the reward (Avot 1:3)
236.hook: Antigonus: be like servants who serve without thought of a reward
236.tomorrow: Sit in the dust of the wise
236.howItsDone: The Talmud teaches that a person should keep doing the commandments even for other motives, because from that they come to do them lishmah, for their own sake.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three pillars: the world stands on learning, worship and deeds of loving-kindness. Your line was three legs to stand on. Did you touch all three? Today, Simon the Just's student speaks. Day two hundred thirty-six.

Gold stars. Points. Streaks. Badges. Employee of the month. Our whole world runs on little rewards, and to be fair, they work. Plenty of us learned to read for a sticker. But watch what can happen when the reward stops. The kid who read for stickers stops reading. The volunteer who wanted to be thanked quits when nobody does. Long ago, a sage named Antigonus, from a town called Socho, looked at this and gave advice that's hard to hear.
screen: `GOLD STARS AND STREAKS.` → `WHEN THE REWARD STOPS.` → `ANTIGONUS OF SOCHO.`

segments.voice: Antigonus received the tradition from Simon the Just, the next link in the chain. His saying, in paraphrase: don't be like servants who serve their master in order to receive a reward. Be like servants who serve their master not in order to receive a reward. And let the awe of heaven be upon you. The Hebrew word for reward here is peras. Some commentators say it means something small: a tip, a treat, a little bonus a master tosses to a servant. Antigonus isn't saying good deeds go unrewarded. He's saying don't make the tip the point. Do the right thing because it's right, and because of who you're serving. There's an old story that shows how easily this can be misheard. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Avot, tells of two students of Antigonus, Zadok and Boethus. They heard, don't serve for a reward, and concluded: then there is no reward, no world to come. And, the story says, they broke away and founded their own sects. Historians doubt the story, but the warning is clear: a saying about motive can be twisted into a saying about emptiness. Later, the philosopher Maimonides made peace with the gold stars. A child, he wrote, is taught first with sweets, then with new clothes, then with coins, and later with honor. That's fine. That's how people start. The goal is to grow, slowly, toward serving out of love. Not for the prize. For the one you serve, and for the good itself.
screen: `SERVE NOT FOR THE REWARD.` · `PERAS — A TIP, A TREAT.` · `TWO STUDENTS WHO MISHEARD.` · `FROM SWEETS TO LOVE.` · then, large: `NOT FOR THE PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with no reward. Settle, and breathe. Think of the good things you did this week. Now notice, honestly, which ones had a little tip attached: a thank-you you were waiting for, a like, a favor owed. That's human; don't scold yourself. Then pick one thing you could do today where no tip is possible. No one will know, no one will thank you. The bell holds the time.
Peras. A reward, a small tip: the word in Antigonus's warning not to serve like a servant who expects one, but with awe of heaven.
Your line: not for the prize. Today, do one good thing and tell no one, not even a hint. Day two hundred thirty-six.

237.title: Sit in the dust of the wise (Avot 1:4)
237.hook: let your house be a meeting place for the wise; drink their words with thirst
237.howItsDone: Some Jews host study sessions and invite teachers into their homes, and traditional learning happens in pairs or small circles close to a teacher, arguing as well as listening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antigonus: serve not for peras. Your line was not for the prize. Did you do one good thing and tell no one? Today, the chain passes to two men named Yose, and the first one talks about dust. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

Two people are learning to fix a car. One watches a repair video at double speed while answering email. The other spends a Saturday in a neighbor's garage, grease on his sleeves, handing over wrenches, asking why, getting told to be quiet and watch. Both are learning. Only one of them is getting dirty. That kind of learning is a little messy. It means getting close, being the least important person in the room, and wanting it badly. An old sage put all of that into one dusty picture. Today: mitabek.
screen: `VIDEO AT DOUBLE SPEED.` → `GREASE ON HIS SLEEVES.` → `LEARNING GETS DIRTY.`

segments.voice: After Antigonus, Avot's chain passes to pairs of teachers. The first pair: Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan. Yose ben Yoezer says three things, in paraphrase. Let your house be a meeting place for the wise. Sit in the dust of their feet. And drink in their words with thirst. Start with the house. Not the synagogue, not the school. Your house. Make your kitchen table a place where wise people want to come and talk. Then the dust. The commentators give two pictures. In the old academies, students sat on the ground while the teacher sat above them, so you'd literally be in the dust at their feet. Or, the students walked behind their teacher on dirt roads, close enough to catch every word, and got covered in the dust his feet kicked up. Either way: humble, close, and a bit dirty. Some readers hear more in the verb. Mitabek comes from avak, dust. When Jacob wrestles a stranger through the night, the Torah's verb is vaye'avek, and Rashi explains it by the dust the two of them kicked up. So for these readers, sitting in the dust of the wise isn't just sitting still. It can mean wrestling with them. Asking hard questions. Pushing back. Last, drink their words with thirst. Not polite sipping. The way you drink after a long run, gulping, grateful. Wisdom goes in best when you really want it. A house that welcomes, a student who gets close, and real thirst.
screen: `YOUR HOUSE, A MEETING PLACE.` · `AT THEIR FEET, OR ON THEIR ROAD.` · `MITABEK — TO WRESTLE IN DUST.` · `DRINK WITH THIRST.` · then, large: `SIT IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from someone older. Settle, and breathe. Think of an older person in your life who knows something you don't. A grandparent, a neighbor, a senior colleague, the old man at the hardware store. What could they teach you? A recipe, a trade, a story, how they got through a hard year. Picture sitting near them, asking, and really listening, thirsty. Decide when you'll ask. The bell holds the time.
Mitabek. Sit, or wrestle, in the dust: the verb behind Yose ben Yoezer's saying to get close to the wise and drink in their words with thirst.
Your line: sit in the dust. Today, ask someone older one real question, then stop talking and listen all the way to the end. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

238.title: A house open wide (Avot 1:5)
238.hook: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household
238.howItsDone: Hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, is a Jewish practice: guests are invited to Shabbat and holiday meals, and early in the seder the Haggadah invites all who are hungry to come and eat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitabek. This first week of camp five opened Pirkei Avot: the chain handed down, judge slowly, three legs to stand on, and not for the prize. Today, the other Yose talks about your front door. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

Some homes you just walk into. The door's unlocked, there's always something on the stove, and nobody asks why you came. Kids from down the street end up at dinner. A cousin sleeps on the couch for a month. Other homes, lovely ones, are closed: you visit by appointment, and you leave before it gets awkward. Plenty of homes are somewhere in between. Yesterday, the first Yose said: let your house be a meeting place for the wise. Today, his partner, Yose from Jerusalem, goes further. Not just the wise. Everyone.
screen: `THE HOUSE YOU JUST WALK INTO.` → `VISITS BY APPOINTMENT.` → `NOT JUST THE WISE.`

segments.voice: Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem says, in paraphrase: let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household. In Hebrew, open wide is patuach lirvacha. Revach means space, room, relief. A house open to spaciousness. A house where someone in trouble can breathe. The rabbis pictured Abraham's tent. A midrash says it had openings on all four sides, so a traveler coming from any direction would find a door facing them. In Genesis, Abraham runs out in the heat of the day to greet three strangers. That's the model. Then the second half: let the poor be members of your household. Not guests at the back door. Not a donation in an envelope. Family. At the table, in the conversation, known by name. Some commentators note the dignity in it: a poor person who's treated like a member of the house doesn't have to feel ashamed to be there. Honesty requires one more note. The same saying continues with a warning against too much idle talk with women, words that some readers today find troubling, and that commentators over the centuries have explained, limited, and argued about. We're not going to pretend it isn't there. But the first line is the one to carry today: an extra chair at Shabbat dinner, a stranger at the seder, a door that opens easily. Wide enough that anyone coming from any direction finds a way in.
